I've recently had a debate with a fellow voat user who did not understand how these things work.

Apparently most people don't know and some are actually spreading misinformation.

So let's clear things up once and for all. :)

"Virtual memory" is not the same as "pagefile". This is the most common misconception.

Virtual memory is a wrapper for RAM and/or pagefile.

A virtual memory address may refer to RAM or pagefile.

The guys & gals who made Windows say so in this article:

Virtual memory combines your computer’s RAM with temporary space on your hard disk. When RAM runs low, virtual memory moves data from RAM to a space called a paging file.

This is so that developers don't have to worry about memory management.

The above is "an expanded version" of another Microsoft article on the matter:

When the memory being used by all the existing processes exceeds the available RAM, the operating system moves pages (4-KB pieces) of one or more virtual address spaces to the computer’s hard disk. This frees that RAM frame for other uses. In Windows systems, these “paged out” pages are stored in one or more files (Pagefile.sys files) in the root of a partition.

So if you disable pagefile the system will only use RAM.

Another thing to keep in mind is that if you have pagefile active it will be used even if you still have enough free RAM:

When RAM is in short supply (for example, Committed Bytes is greater than installed RAM), the operating system will try to keep a certain fraction of installed RAM available for immediate use by copying virtual memory pages that are not in active use to the pagefile.

I personally prefer to keep the pagefile disabled since the HDD is the biggest bottle-neck in any system.

tl;dr

"Virtual memory" is not the same as "pagefile".

Virtual memory is a wrapper for RAM and/or pagefile.

The pagefile is used when RAM is running low.

If you disable the pagefile your system will only use RAM.
[windows] virtual memory, RAM and the ever mysterious "pagefile"
I don't know If this is true for Windows, but some operating systems use swap (like pagefiles) for hibernation. There are definately reasons to not disable it even if you have plenty of memory.
Windows has a specific file for this: hiberfil.sys .

Once upon a time they were more or less synonymous, even though they were only semi-related. Because you can't page out memory to the hard drive without virtual memory addressing. These days where it's easy to have a system with 8G of memory and nothing should use that much unless it's written like crap, virtual memory is still used to keep a program's memory contiguous. In some operating systems this cannot occur unless there is a swap file. Back in the XP days, setting 0 swap would cause problems, so you had to set a 2MB swap file.

I still encounter people calling the hard drive "memory" which was correct, or at least common 30+ years ago, but terms have evolved with computing. You just have to deal with it because some people are outdated and some people are clueless. I know people who call anything that's not the monitor/keyboard/mouse the "hard drive" or call any small networking box (like routers, hubs, etc) the "modem". You won't fix them.
